analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with high-risk pools, interstate insurance sales, and malpractice caps.
analysis.headline: The repeal bill, backed by one sponsor and one cosponsor, never received a hearing or a vote and died in House committees when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the 2010 reconciliation law in full, then replace them with a partial set of protections: state-run high-risk pools for people denied coverage, a ban on annual and lifetime dollar caps, and a few retained rules. At the same time it would deregulate insurance — letting plans sell across state lines under the insurer's home state's rules and through association plans that override state rating laws — expand health savings accounts, create new tax deductions for health premiums, and cap malpractice awards.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed: health insurers, which would shed minimum-benefit standards, rating limits, and medical-loss-ratio rules while gaining the right to sell coverage governed by their home state's laws; trade associations and chambers of commerce, which could sponsor health plans that preempt state rules; self-employed and higher-income taxpayers, who would get new deductions for health premiums; and physicians and malpractice insurers, who would benefit from caps on damages. People with preexisting conditions would get access to state high-risk pools, but pool premiums could run up to 150% of the standard rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, associations, self-employed and higher earners

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to run a high-risk pool covering people with preexisting conditions, with no waiting periods, premiums capped at 150% of the standard rate, and $15 billion plus an additional $10 billion in federal funding.
Prohibits insurers from applying annual or lifetime aggregate spending caps to any coverage or plan.
Keeps two ACA protections for group health plans: dependent coverage until age 26 and a ban on preexisting-condition exclusions for children under 19.
Creates an independent external review before an insurer can cancel (rescind) individual coverage, with coverage staying in force during the review.

Expands health savings accounts, including allowing premiums for high-deductible plans to be paid from the accounts, and lets self-employed people and individuals deduct health insurance costs in computing income tax.
Caps non-economic damages in malpractice cases, requires expert reports and actively-practicing physicians as experts, and requires unanimous juries for punitive damages.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed: the millions of people whose coverage depended on ACA premium subsidies and the Medicaid expansion, which the bill repeals outright; adults with preexisting conditions outside group plans, who would depend on state pools that can charge up to 150% of standard premiums and that states must partly fund from their own premium assessments; consumers in states whose rating and benefit laws would be overridden when insurers sell in from other states or through association plans; and people injured by medical negligence, whose recoverable damages would be capped.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA subsidy and Medicaid-expansion enrollees; malpractice claimants

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the ACA and the 2010 reconciliation law in full, eliminating premium tax credits, the Medicaid expansion, and the ban on preexisting-condition exclusions for adults outside the new high-risk pools.
It lets insurers sell coverage across state lines under the laws of their home ('primary') state, preempting the consumer protections and rating rules of the state where the customer lives.

It preempts state rating and benefit laws for certified small business health plans run by trade associations and chambers of commerce, and lets plans set their own benefit designs and rates based on claims experience.
It allows premiums and cost-sharing to vary by up to 50% based on participation in a wellness program, raising costs for people who cannot participate.
It caps non-economic and, in wrongful-death cases, total damages in malpractice suits, limiting compensation for patients injured by medical errors.
The retained age-26 dependent coverage and under-19 preexisting-condition protections apply only to group plans, not to individual coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill keeps a few popular protections and puts real money ($25 billion) behind high-risk pools, but its core effect is to undo the ACA's coverage expansion and replace it with mechanisms — state pools, tax deductions, cross-state sales — that historically cover far fewer people at higher out-of-pocket cost, with the new tax deductions skewing toward higher earners and the deregulation provisions shifting rulemaking power from states to insurers' home states. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the replacement does not reach most of the people the repealed provisions did.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees, then to three subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Latham (R-IA) introduced the bill on September 20, 2013.
It was referred to eight House committees: Energy and Commerce (lead), plus Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Judiciary, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations.

In the following weeks it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, the Natural Resources Indian and Alaska Native Affairs Subcommittee, and the Judiciary Constitution and Civil Justice Subcommittee.
It attracted one cosponsor, a Republican.
No committee took up the bill and no vote was ever held; the last recorded action was the January 9, 2014 subcommittee referral, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act's subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and consumer protections remained in place for the people who relied on them; insurers, associations, and higher earners who would have gained from repeal did not. No one acted to stop the bill — it simply was never a priority in the Republican-led House, which pursued other ACA-repeal vehicles.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People keeping ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Tom Latham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to eight committees.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote in the committee that received it first.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the single cosponsor were Republicans; the bill never advanced even in the Republican-led House, where leadership pursued other repeal bills instead.

industries.note: Repeal would remove minimum-benefit standards, rating limits, and medical-loss-ratio rules, and the bill would let insurers sell under their home state's rules and override state rating laws through association plans. The public backstop for the sickest customers shifts to state high-risk pools partly funded by state money.

industries.industry: Trade associations and chambers of commerce
industries.note: The bill creates a new ERISA channel for association-sponsored small business health plans certified federally, preempting state rating and benefit requirements. Members gain pooled coverage options, but the plans can skim healthier groups and override state consumer rules.

New deductions for health insurance premiums against self-employment income and gross income reduce taxes for people who buy their own coverage, with the largest benefit going to those in higher tax brackets; the ACA's income-based subsidies, which they would lose, are worth more to lower earners.

Damage caps, expert-witness requirements, and shorter filing deadlines would cut malpractice exposure and premiums. The cost falls on patients with serious injuries, whose recoverable damages would be limited.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers and medical device makers
industries.note: Repealing the ACA in full would end the law's annual fee on brand-name prescription drugs and its excise tax on medical devices, removing costs those industries had been paying; consumers would not get a corresponding benefit.

Each state would be required to run a qualifying high-risk pool and apply state funds, including premium assessments, to it, while the same bill preempts state rating and licensure authority for insurers selling in from other states or through certified association plans.
